Fitted Model — Tutorial Edition

A statistically-honest reading of HRE city growth, 1200–1500. Reads every metric from scratch; reports five model variants from weakest to strongest.

What This Report Does

You asked two things: (1) build a stronger equation for HRE city growth, and (2) explain the statistics from scratch because the graphs are not intuitive. This report tries to do both. Every section starts with plain English; the math is right next to it but optional.

The headline finding, before any math: R² ≈ 1 is not achievable here, ever. Reasonable ceilings for this kind of historical data are 0.6–0.85 for predicting a city's level of population and 0.15–0.30 for predicting its growth rate. We get into why in §2 and §6.

1. Stats Primer — Read This Once

Regression in one sentence

Regression draws a line (or surface, in higher dimensions) through a cloud of points to give the best linear guess of an outcome from one or more inputs.

1.1 What R² actually means

R² answers: compared to just guessing the average, how much does my model reduce prediction error?

  • R² = 0 — the model is no better than always predicting the mean. Useless.
  • R² = 0.5 — the model has cut squared prediction error in half versus the mean.
  • R² = 1.0 — perfect prediction. Every dot lands exactly on the line.
  • R² < 0 — the model is worse than guessing the mean. Happens when you train on one regime and test on a different one.

Worked example. Suppose 5 cities have actual log(pop) = [7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. The mean is 9. Total squared error from "always guess 9" is 4+1+0+1+4 = 10. A model predicts [7.5, 8.2, 9.1, 9.8, 10.9]. Its squared error is 0.25+0.04+0.01+0.04+0.01 = 0.35. So R² = 1 − 0.35/10 = 0.965. Clean fit.

Why R² = 1 is impossible in this dataset.
  1. Bairoch records population in steps of 1,000. A 5,000-person town could be 4,500 or 5,499 — that rounding alone caps achievable R² at ~0.95 even with a perfect model.
  2. Cities grew or shrank because of plague variance, individual rulers, fires, harvest shocks, marriage politics — none of these are in any of our 6 factors. They show up as residual noise.
  3. Bairoch sometimes lists a town in 1500 but not in 1400, or vice versa, which means our panel is biased toward already-large cities. Smaller towns whose fortunes whip around the most are missing.

1.2 In-sample vs out-of-sample (the overfitting trap)

If I fit a model to N data points and then ask how well it fits those same N points, I will always look smart — even a deliberately bad model can memorise. The honest test is to hold out some data the model never sees, then ask how well it predicts those.

  • In-sample R² — fit and evaluate on the same data. Almost always optimistic; rises whenever you add features.
  • k-fold cross-validation R² (CV R²) — split the cities into k=5 groups; train on 4, test on the 5th; rotate. We report the average across folds. This is a fair measure of how well the model would do on cities it never saw.
  • Temporal-holdout R² — train on early periods, test on a late period. Even fairer, but if the late period is a regime shift (e.g., post-Black-Death recovery), this can be very pessimistic.

1.3 Coefficients (β) and their confidence intervals

Each factor has a coefficient β. After we z-score the factors (subtract mean, divide by SD), β tells you: per +1 standard deviation of this factor, the outcome moves by β units, holding the others fixed.

Bootstrap 95% CI: if we re-collected and re-fit the data many times, 95% of estimates would land in this interval. If the CI excludes zero we say the effect is "statistically significant" — meaning we are confident about the sign, not the size.

Reading a calibration plot

  • X-axis: the actual outcome.
  • Y-axis: the model's prediction.
  • The dashed line is y = x — perfect prediction.
  • Points on the line: good. Points scattered: noisy. Points on a different slope: model has bias.
  • Tighter cloud → higher R². The R² value is printed in the title.

Reading a residual map

  • Each dot is a city, plotted at its actual lat/lon.
  • Color = residual = actual − predicted. Blue means the model under-predicted (city was bigger than expected). Red means over-predicted.
  • What you want: random colors with no spatial pattern (just noise).
  • What you don't want: all the south is red and all the north is blue → model is missing a regional factor and is biased.

2. The Data

Two panels are constructed:

  • Level panel. One row per (city, year) for years {1300, 1400, 1500} where Bairoch population exists AND population 100 years earlier exists. Outcome: log(pop_T). n = 749 rows from 260 cities.
  • Growth panel. One row per (city, transition) for transitions {1200→1300, 1300→1400, 1400→1500}. Outcome: Δlog(pop) over 100 years. n = 513 rows.

2.1 What the outcome looks like

A handful of huge cities, lots of small ones. The raw distribution is extremely skewed.

After log-transforming, the distribution is roughly bell-shaped. Linear regression assumes the outcome is roughly bell-shaped, which is why we model log(pop) — not pop directly.

Δlog(pop) is the 100-year growth rate. Mean ≈ +0.09 (so on average cities grew ≈ +9.0% over 100 years). The spread is large, which is exactly why R² is hard.

3. Five Model Variants — Watch R² Climb

Each variant adds something. Watch the CV R² rise.

Headline. The dominant predictor of city size at year T is city size at year T−100. Adding it (Model B) takes CV R² from 0.29 to 0.75. This is not cheating — it is asking a different question. Model A asks "given factors alone, predict size". Model B asks "given factors AND prior size, predict size". Model E asks the hardest one: "given factors, predict growth".

3.1 Model A — Factors only (level)

log(pop_T) = α + Σ β_k · z(factor_k at T) + year_FE

Plain English. "Given a city's six factor scores at year T, and which year T is, predict log(pop) at T." No information about prior size.

3.2 Model B — Add prior population (the strong baseline)

log(pop_T) = α + β_lag · log(pop_T-100) + Σ β_k · z(factor_k at T) + year_FE

Plain English. "Given a city's size 100 years ago, plus its six factor scores today, predict its size today."

This is the equation I would recommend when you want a real predictive model with high R². The lag-pop term (β = +0.843) is doing most of the work — cities with a large population in 1400 tend to have a large population in 1500. The factors then tweak that prediction up or down.

Coefficient plot

After controlling for prior size, several factor coefficients shrink toward zero — not because they don't matter, but because their effect is mostly absorbed by lag-pop (a city's factors and its prior size are themselves correlated). The factors that still have significant CIs after this are the ones with predictive power beyond autocorrelation.

3.4 Model D — Random Forest (non-linear ceiling)

Plain English. A Random Forest is a non-linear model — it can learn step functions, sharp thresholds, multi-way interactions all at once. If a flexible model does much better than the linear one, the linear model was leaving fit on the table. If they tie, our linear equation is already capturing what the data can support.

Coefficients

The factors that significantly drive growth (CI excludes zero) are where you should focus your interpretation. The lag-pop term is negative (~-0.235): mean reversion — already-big cities grow slower over the next 100 years.

4. The Recommended Equation

If you want one equation to use, this is it (Model B):

log(pop_T) = α + β_lag · log(pop_T-100) + β_legal · z(legal_capacity) + β_merchant · z(merchant_capital) + β_trade · z(trade_access) + β_agri · z(agricultural_surplus) + β_noble · z(noble_extraction) + β_conflict · z(conflict_risk) + γ_year (year fixed effect)

Fitted values (in-sample R² = 0.757, k-fold CV R² = 0.750 ± 0.021):

  • α = +1.5330
  • β_lag = +0.8429
  • β_legal_capacity = +0.0857
  • β_merchant_capital = +0.0712
  • β_agricultural_surplus = -0.0218
  • β_noble_extraction = +0.0223
  • β_conflict_risk = +0.0130
  • β_trade_access = -0.0191
  • γ_1400 (vs 1300) = -0.5248
  • γ_1500 (vs 1300) = +0.0163

5. Why R² Isn't Higher (And What Would Help)

Three concrete reasons R² in §3 is bounded:

5.1 Measurement noise in the outcome

Bairoch reports population in thousands. The true population can be anywhere within a 1,000-person bucket. For a 5,000-person town that's ±10%, which on the log scale is roughly ±0.1. The total variance of log(pop) in our panel is about 0.77; rounding noise alone consumes some of that variance, capping achievable R² below 1.

5.2 Unobserved shocks

Cities grew or shrank because of factors none of our 6 measures cover: plague mortality variance, individual rulers, religious orders moving in, royal favoritism, harvest shocks, fires. These show up as irreducible residual noise. Many of these are basically random with respect to the slow-moving structural factors we have.

5.3 Selection bias

Bairoch only lists cities once they reach a certain size. The most interesting growth — small village to medium town — is invisible. Cities that shrank below the threshold drop out. Both biases trim the most volatile cases from our panel.

5.4 Linear specification

The Random Forest in §3.4 is a sanity check: if it dramatically beats the linear model, our linear equation is leaving fit on the table. Here RF CV R² ≈ 0.74 vs Model B's ≈ 0.75. RF does not meaningfully beat the linear model — most of the predictable variance is linear, and adding model flexibility won't help much.

6. What You Could Provide to Push R² Higher

Honest list, in order of expected R² lift:

  1. Annual or decadal population data instead of 100-year snapshots (≈ +0.10–0.20 R²). Bairoch's 100-year jumps average over multi-generation dynamics. If you have a city-level annual census even for a subset (e.g., Hanseatic city Bürgerbücher, Imperial tax rolls 1437/1521, Italian catasti), they would let us capture intra-century trends.
  2. Geographic features we don't currently have (≈ +0.05–0.10 R²). Specifically: distance to nearest sea coast or navigable port; soil-quality classes (FAO HWSD raster data); elevation contour for hinterland; Roman-road network density. All derivable from public GIS, but none currently in /docs.
  3. Climate / harvest variation (≈ +0.05 R²). Late Medieval Warm Period vs Little Ice Age effects on agricultural surplus. Tree-ring summer-temperature reconstructions exist (Büntgen et al.) at decadal resolution.
  4. Wealth or trade-volume proxies (≈ +0.05 R²). Sound Toll registers (already in /docs but post-1497), Hanseatic shipping records, mint output, Italian bank ledgers.
  5. A "shock" indicator capturing big plague years, major sieges, or city sackings beyond our coarse conflict_risk score. Even a hand-curated list of 1346–53 plague mortality by city would help.
  6. Decisions you can make now without new data:
    • Should the model predict levels or growth? Levels give higher R² (Model B) but are dominated by lag pop; growth gives smaller R² but cleaner causal interpretation.
    • Should we use a non-linear model (Random Forest, gradient boosting) as the headline? Better fit, less interpretable coefficients.
    • Are there specific cities whose history you'd like the model to fit better? We can up-weight them in training, at the cost of overall fit elsewhere.
Realistic R² ceiling for this question — even with everything in #1–5 above, I would not expect CV R² above ~0.85 for levels and ~0.30 for growth. Beyond that point, the residual variance is genuinely random with respect to anything observable at city-level in this period.

7. Appendix — Files & How to Re-Run

  • build_fitted_model_report.py — this script. Reads the per-factor *_continuous columns and Bairoch population.
  • lib/bairoch_pop.py — canonical Bairoch panel loader (city_id ↔ name+spatial match).
  • output/cities_*_continuous columns inside each per-factor CSV — the un-bucketed factor signal each builder now emits.
  • output/cities_trade_access_bairoch.csv — Bairoch-keyed trade access with south-German fallback (so Augsburg, Ulm, Würzburg, Regensburg, Bamberg, Speyer, Rothenburg are no longer zero).

Re-run end-to-end: python3 build_all.py then python3 build_fitted_model_report.py. Re-running this script alone takes ≈30 s.
